Nicéphore Niépce. A French inventor who created the first permanent photograph using a process called heliography around 1822. Though he did not live to see photography's commercial success, his pioneering work on light-sensitive materials and camera obscura techniques directly enabled Louis Daguerre's later triumph.

Niépce produced View from the Window at Le Gras around 1822, considered the oldest surviving permanent photograph. It was taken with an eight-hour exposure through a camera obscura onto a bitumen-coated pewter plate. He used bitumen of Judea, a light-sensitive tar-like substance, as his recording medium. It hardened when exposed to light and could be washed away to create an image. Niépce coined the term heliography—meaning light-writing—for his process. However, the process required extremely long exposures, rendering it impractical for portraiture.

In 1829 Niépce partnered with Louis Daguerre to refine his process. After Niépce's death in 1833, Daguerre continued alone and perfected a faster, more practical approach that became the daguerreotype. Niépce worked in rural Burgundy, France, largely in isolation. This makes his achievements even more remarkable given the lack of scientific community surrounding him at the time.

His conceptual and technical work inspired William Henry Fox Talbot, the contemporary English inventor pursuing similar goals independently, which led to the calotype process. Yet Niépce and Talbot's thinking diverged sharply from the aesthetic concerns of Alfred Stieglitz, the later photographer whose artistic vision contrasted with the technical focus of the Niépce-Daguerre era.
